The treatment of vestibular schwannomas has undergone numerous changes and 
advancements in the past century. Innovations in surgical and now microsurgical 
techniques allow for the removal of these lesions with the preservation of nearby 
cranial nerves in the majority of cases. In addition, the development of stereotactic 
radiation can provide disease control in a min

on [60–62]. 
Additionally, facial nerve tumors often involve multiple segments with the most 
common being the geniculate ganglion and demonstrate enhancement on MRI or 
bony changes to the fallopian canal beyond what can be expected for primary VS [60, 
61, 63, 64]. However, in lesions that resemble primary VS (facial nerve schwanno-
mas limited to the IAC and CPA), the symptom profile is typically indistinguishable 
from primary VS with typically no evidence of facial nerve dysfunction [58, 59]. 
Often, the intraoperative clue that the surgeon has encountered a primary facial nerve 
lesion is that there is no tissue plane between the lesion and the facial nerve. The 
entire substance of the lesion will often stimulate with the facial nerve stimulating 
electrode. Sometimes, with small or medially based lesions, the facial nerve can be 
traced medially from the meatal foramen and the lesion and nerve become one entity.

Vestibular schwannomas (VS) are benign, extra-axial, encapsulated, Schwann cell 
derived neoplasms of the vestibular part of the eighth cranial nerve. Although some 
earlier reports indicated that the superior vestibular nerve is the more common ori-
gin of VS, recent studies suggest otherwise. Sanna et al. found that the most com-
mon origin for VS are the nerve sheath of the inferior vestibular nerve, and less 
frequently the superior vestibular nerve [1]. Eighth cranial nerve schwannomas rep-
resent 90% of all intracranial nerve sheath tumors [2]. VS account for approxi-
mately 6–8% of intracranial tumors in adults [3, 4] and are the most common tumor 
in the cerebellopontine angle (CPA) ranging between 80% and 95% [5, 6], followed 
by meningiomas ranging between 5% and 10% and epidermoid tumors ranging 
between 4% and 7% [7–9]. There are two types of VS; sporadic and familial. The

The surgery and postoperative course were uneventful. Postoperative MRI 
showed gross total resection of the tumor (Fig. 6.5a, b). The histopathology was a 
schwannoma. The patient’s facial nerve function immediately after surgery was 
House-Brackmann grade II on the left side, which improved to grade I in 2 weeks 
and remained grade I bilaterally at 18-month follow-up.
This case is presented to demonstrate that some large VSs, especially in young 
patients such as this 23-year old, can be quite vascular, thereby causing difficulties 
with hemostasis. Hypervascularity of the tumor and its capsule in the porus and 
internal acoustic canal locations are due to rich meningeal feeders coming from the 
dura of the internal acoustic canal. As demonstrated in the video of this case, 
extreme care should be exercised not to use high-level bipolar coagulation near the 
facial nerve, and that only side feeders should be taken.

Anatomy

tion relative to surrounding neurovascular structures. Schwannomas can arise from 
other nerves in the region and present with similar symptoms but these are uncom-
mon and beyond the scope of this textbook. VSs are benign tumors that arise from 
the superior or inferior vestibular nerves. These nerves originate from the lateral 
aspect of the brainstem, traverse the cerebellopontine angle (CPA) cistern and the

Intraoperative Monitoring
Depending on the goals of surgery and the surgical approach selected by the patient 
and surgeon, various cranial nerves may be monitored during the operation. The

Cranial Nerve VII

tumors. Its main uses include monitoring for possible facial nerve (FN) injury and 
physiologic identification in situations where the FN anatomy has been significantly 
altered. However, FNM does not replace the detailed anatomic knowledge and tech-
nical skill required to operate near the facial nerve.

this pathology. “Vestibular” clearly indicates the origin of the tumor as from the 
vestibular nerve, while “schwannoma” indicates that Schwann cells are the cell

Introduction
Since the technical description by William House [1] in 1961, the middle cranial 
fossa (MCF) approach to the internal acoustic canal (IAC) has become one of the 
quintessential surgical approaches for accessing the 7th and 8th cranial nerves and 
the upper cerebellopontine angle (CPA). Though many variations have been 
described, in this chapter the MCF approach comprises an extradural, subtemporal 
exposure and removal of a portion of the superior surface of the temporal bone to 
expose the posterior cranial fossa (PCF) structures. The technique affords access to 
the entire contents of the internal acoustic canal (IAC) and can allow for hearing 
preservation by avoiding violation of the otic capsule during the surgical exposure.
